title: World's Smallest Crocodiles Caught on Camera Hunting Bats in a Cave
summary:
Imagine a cave so dark you can't see your hand in front of your face. The floor is squishy — not mud, but a thick layer of bat poop. And somewhere in there, crocodiles are hunting.

That's the scene in Gabon's Abanda Caves, where a unique group of dwarf crocodiles — the world's smallest croc species, only about 5 feet long — has been living underground for possibly thousands of years. Scientists knew the crocs were eating bats and insects, but they'd never actually seen them hunt. The crocs would hide whenever people came near.

Now, using special remote cameras, a team has captured video of the crocodiles sneaking up and snatching bats out of the air. It's a behavior never seen before.

"I've been working with this population for almost 15 or 16 years, and that's something we've never been able to see," said Matt Shirley, a conservation ecologist.

Life in the cave is extreme. The crocs swim through bat guano (that's the fancy word for poop), which is acidic and actually tans their skin, turning it orange. But there's a plus side: the cave has lots of prey and no predators, so the crocodiles are often better fed than their forest cousins.

Because they stay in the cave and only mate with each other, they're becoming genetically different from other dwarf crocodiles. "It's very 'Jurassic Park,'" Shirley said. "This is evolution in action."
why_it_matters: It shows that animals can surprise us in places we have barely looked, and that even a dark, smelly cave can be the home of something truly special.

background_read: Gabon is a country on the west coast of Africa, covered in thick rainforest — and it is home to these rare cave crocodiles.
Dwarf crocodiles are the smallest living crocodile species. Most of them hunt at night in forests and would hide when people came close, so scientists almost never got to see them catch food.
Caves are extreme places: no sunlight means food has to fly or fall in, like bats do, and animals that stay underground for thousands of years can slowly become a new, separate group.
Article_Structure: WHO: A team led by conservation ecologist Matt Shirley, who has studied this crocodile group for almost 15 or 16 years.
WHAT: Remote cameras filmed dwarf crocodiles sneaking up and snatching bats out of the air — a hunting behavior never seen before.
WHERE: The Abanda Caves in Gabon, where the crocs swim through acidic bat guano that tans their skin orange.
WHY: Because the crocodiles stay in the cave and only mate with each other, they are becoming genetically different from other dwarf crocodiles — evolution happening right now.

perspectives.description: This is a hunting behavior never seen before, which proves the cave crocodiles are specialized hunters in their strange underground world.
Because they live in just one cave and only breed with each other, a single disaster there could wipe the whole group out.
The crocodiles seem to be doing fine — the cave gives them plenty of prey and no predators, so they are often better fed than their forest cousins.
